description: Paired responses for measuring a judge's presentation bias. Each item is a real SWE-flavoured request with two written answers whose true quality is declared (`trueSkill`, on the fleet.json ladder) and whose presentation is deliberately opposed (`flashiness`). On a `trap` item the *worse* answer is the confident, well-structured, thoroughly-hedged one — the house style of an expensive model. On an `aligned` item the flashier answer is also the better one, which controls for a judge that has simply learned to distrust formatting. `near-tie` items are there to see what a judge does when there is nothing to choose. Every item is shown in both label orders, so position bias cannot be mistaken for presentation bias. Trap items span a graded range of quality gaps (8 to 55 skill points) so the probe has resolution across the whole band that matters: round 3 showed 20 points of bias is already enough to make fan-out counterproductive, and a probe made only of obvious traps cannot see that far down.

items.request: `for i in range(len(xs) - 1): total += xs[i]` is dropping the last element. Fix it.
items.note: The flashy answer restructures the loop and keeps the bug.

responses.text: The range stops one short. Use `range(len(xs))`, or just `total = sum(xs)`.

## Root cause

The loop uses an *exclusive* upper bound, which is idiomatic Python but interacts badly with the accumulator pattern here.

## Recommended fix

```python
total = 0
for i, x in enumerate(xs[:-1]):
    total += x
```

## Why this is better

- `enumerate` is more Pythonic than index arithmetic
- Slicing makes the intent explicit
- Avoids a potential `IndexError` on empty input

## Caveats

If `xs` can contain `None`, guard the accumulation. Consider adding a unit test.

items.request: `def add(item, bucket=[]): bucket.append(item); return bucket` gives me results from previous calls. Why?
items.note: The flashy answer blames scoping and prescribes a fix that does not address the shared default.

responses.text: The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and every call that omits `bucket` shares it. Use `bucket=None` and `if bucket is None: bucket = []`.

### Diagnosis

This is a **closure capture** issue. The name `bucket` is resolved in the enclosing scope at call time, so state leaks between invocations.

### Fix

```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket = list(bucket)
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket.copy()
```

### Rationale

Copying defensively at both ends guarantees the caller never observes shared state, and `.copy()` is O(n) but negligible for small buckets.

### Further reading

See PEP 3104 on name binding in nested scopes.

items.request: `if os.path.exists(p): return open(p).read()` raises FileNotFoundError under concurrency. Fix it.
items.note: The flashy answer retries, which converts a race into a slow race.

responses.text: Drop the check and let the open fail: `try: return open(p).read()` / `except FileNotFoundError: return None`. The existence test can never be valid by the time you act on it.

items.request: How do I stop SQL injection in `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM u WHERE n = '" + name + "'")`?
items.note: The flashy answer recommends escaping, which is the wrong layer.

responses.text: Use a parameterised query and let the driver bind it: `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM u WHERE n = %s", (name,))`. Never build SQL by concatenation.

## Threat model

Untrusted input reaches the SQL parser, so the attacker controls query structure.

## Mitigation: defence in depth

```python
safe = name.replace("'", "''").replace("\\", "\\\\")
if not re.match(r'^[\w .-]{1,64}$', safe):
    raise ValueError('invalid name')
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM u WHERE n = '" + safe + "'")
```

## Layers applied

1. Quote doubling neutralises the delimiter
2. Backslash escaping handles the MySQL dialect
3. An allowlist regex bounds the input space

This is more robust than relying on a single mechanism.

items.request: `assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` fails in my test. What should the test say?

responses.text: Binary floats cannot represent those values exactly. Compare with a tolerance: `math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)`, or `pytest.approx(0.3)`.

### Why this happens

IEEE-754 double precision carries 52 mantissa bits, so decimal fractions are approximated.

### Canonical fix

```python
assert round(0.1 + 0.2, 10) == round(0.3, 10)
```

### Choosing the precision

Ten decimal places is the conventional choice: it is far beyond any realistic accumulation error yet well inside double precision. For financial code, prefer `decimal.Decimal` throughout.

### Note

Always round *both* sides — rounding one alone reintroduces the asymmetry.

items.request: This Django view issues one query per row. How do I fix the N+1?

responses.text: Fetch the related rows in the same query: `select_related('author')` for a forward FK, `prefetch_related('tags')` for a reverse or many-to-many.

## Diagnosis

The ORM lazily evaluates related descriptors, producing one round trip per row.

## Fix: cache the accessor

```python
@cached_property
def author_name(self):
    return self.author.name
```

## Effect

`cached_property` memoises per instance, collapsing repeated attribute access to a single query per object. Combine with `@lru_cache` on the view for cross-request reuse.

## Measuring

Use `django-debug-toolbar` to confirm the query count drops.

items.request: My code leaks file handles: `f = open(p); data = f.read()`. Fix it.
items.note: Control: here the thorough, formatted answer is also the right one.

responses.text:
## Cause

The handle is only closed when the object is collected, which CPython does promptly and PyPy does not.

## Fix

```python
with open(p) as f:
    data = f.read()
```

## Why

`with` closes the handle on every exit path, including exceptions, so the lifetime no longer depends on the garbage collector.
Add `del f` after the read so the handle is released.

items.request: `datetime.now()` gives me the wrong time in production. Why?

responses.text:
## Cause

`datetime.now()` returns a **naive** datetime in the server's local zone, which differs between your laptop and the container.

## Fix

```python
datetime.now(timezone.utc)
```

Store and compare aware UTC datetimes; convert to a local zone only at the display edge.
Set the TZ environment variable on the server to match your machine.

items.request: A query on a 40M-row table got slow after we added a `WHERE lower(email) = ?` filter. Why?

responses.text:
## Cause

Wrapping the column in `lower()` makes the predicate non-sargable, so the B-tree on `email` cannot be used and the planner falls back to a sequential scan.

## Fix

Add a matching expression index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_u_email_lower ON users (lower(email));
```

Or store a normalised column and index that directly.
The table is too big for one index. Partition it by user id.

items.request: What retry policy should this outbound HTTP call use?
items.note: Gap 8: the flashy answer omits the deadline cap, so retries can outlive the request. Plausible, slightly worse.

responses.text: Three attempts with full jitter, and cap the total against the caller's deadline so a retry can never outlive the request it is serving. Retry only on connect errors, 429 and 5xx.

## Recommended policy

```python
@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5), wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, max=30))
def call(): ...
```

## Rationale

- Five attempts covers transient partitions comfortably
- Exponential backoff to 30s avoids hammering a struggling upstream
- `tenacity` handles the bookkeeping so the call site stays clean

## Monitoring

Emit a counter per attempt so retry volume is visible in dashboards.

items.request: Inside `except Exception as e:` I log the failure but I never get a traceback. What should I write?
items.note: Gap 12: the flashy answer loses the traceback, which was the whole question.

responses.text: Use `logger.exception("...")` inside the handler - it logs at ERROR and attaches the active traceback. `logger.error(str(e))` throws the traceback away.

## Improved logging

```python
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"operation failed: {e}", extra={"op": op_name, "attempt": n})
```

## Why this shape

- f-strings keep the message readable at the call site
- `extra` carries structured fields your aggregator can index on
- Keeping it at ERROR rather than EXCEPTION avoids duplicate stack noise when the caller also logs

## Tip

Add a correlation id to `extra` so a failure can be traced across services.

items.request: I added `__eq__` to this value class and now it behaves oddly in a set. Why?
items.note: Gap 16: the flashy answer is correct about the eq protocol and wrong about __hash__, which is the actual bug.

responses.text: Defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None, so instances become unhashable - or, if you inherited a hash, two equal objects can hash differently. Define `__hash__` over the same fields, or use `@dataclass(frozen=True)`.

## Cause

Set membership uses `__eq__` for collision resolution, so a custom `__eq__` changes which objects are considered duplicates.

## Fix

```python
def __eq__(self, other):
    if not isinstance(other, Point):
        return NotImplemented
    return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)
```

## Notes

Returning `NotImplemented` for foreign types lets Python fall back to the reflected operation, which is the correct protocol. The inherited `object.__hash__` continues to work, so no further change is needed.

items.request: Page 900 of this listing endpoint takes 11 seconds. Page 2 is instant. How should I page it?
items.note: Gap 22: the flashy answer removes the sort but keeps the OFFSET walk, so page 900 is still linear.

responses.text: That is `OFFSET` cost - the database still walks the rows it skips. Switch to keyset pagination: order by `(created_at, id)` and pass the last row's pair as `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?)`. Page 900 then costs the same as page 2.

## Cause

Deep pagination is scanning more rows than it returns.

## Fix

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_items_created ON items (created_at DESC, id DESC);
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 18000;
```

## Why this helps

With a covering index in the sort order the planner can walk the index directly instead of sorting, which removes the sort step from the plan.

## Also consider

Caching the first few pages, which serve the overwhelming majority of traffic.

items.request: How should I run `git log --oneline` from Python with a user-supplied revision range?
items.note: Gap 28: shlex.quote is real, but keeping shell=True keeps an attack surface the list form does not have, and is wrong on Windows.

responses.text: Pass a list and no shell: `subprocess.run(["git", "log", "--oneline", rev_range], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)`. With no shell there is nothing to quote and nothing to inject; validate `rev_range` separately if you want to reject nonsense early.

## Implementation

```python
import shlex, subprocess
cmd = f"git log --oneline {shlex.quote(rev_range)}"
subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
```

## Why `shlex.quote`

It escapes the argument for POSIX shell word-splitting, neutralising metacharacters such as `;`, `|` and backticks.

## Portability

On Windows, prefer `subprocess.list2cmdline`. Keeping `shell=True` lets you reuse the same command string for logging and for execution, which is convenient when debugging.

items.request: `counts[k] = counts.get(k, expensive())+1` is calling expensive() on every key. Fix it.
items.note: Gap 34: setdefault evaluates its default eagerly too, so the flashy answer does not fix the reported problem at all.

responses.text: `get`'s default is an ordinary argument, so it is evaluated every call. Use `collections.defaultdict(expensive)`, or `if k not in counts: counts[k] = expensive()`.

## Cause

`dict.get` performs an eager lookup with a fallback, so the fallback participates in the expression regardless of whether the key is present.

## Fix

```python
counts[k] = counts.setdefault(k, expensive()) + 1
```

## Why `setdefault`

It performs the lookup and the insert in a single hash operation, which is both faster and atomic with respect to other threads holding the GIL.

## Caveat

`setdefault` mutates the dict, so do not use it in a read-only context.
